blocks.x: It's working now. Let's get your name first. Yours is turning. Yours is turning?
Okay, it's turning. Okay. Dick Allen, my name is Harold Peterson.
And where are we at?
Senior, we at 3518 Elysian Field, the home of the Petersons, for him and Harold. Now I'm going to give you a little bit about my dad, George S. Peterson.
Okay.
George S. Peterson was a virtue, he was born about 1875. George S. Peterson was a virtuous of the percussion. He played at the Tulane Theater for about 35 years. Also timpanish at the Sanger Theater.

Dick Denner went to work out at a place called the Peking Inn out in Bucktown. It was Chinese food, you know. Well out in Bucktown, you know, the big thing that people went out there for was to play the slot machines, you know, and dance and of course, Sproonings was more or less a fine rest, a family type of restaurant, Sproonings was, and of course people used to come out there to dance, you know what I mean, and play the slot machines and that's what they had all out there in Bucktown was slot machines, a lot of people went out there for that. So I went to work for well, it's Chinese food, the Peking Inn, and after I worked for them all quite a while, then one night they came to me and they had two bosses, the piano player was a half owner, and he said to me, you know man, he said we can get a piano player and a drummer and the drummer sings for them, just what would we pay you? I said, well man, you know I don't sing, I said, so you're going to have to get you that piano player and drummer. So then I took a band myself over the Tom's Roadhouse, I couldn't get a union musician to go out there either, it was on the West End Shell Road, so I had to get some non-union musicians to work with me out there, but there used to be other musicians to come in and sit in, you know, sit in, and Raymond used to, Raymond talks about it every night, he said, you remember when I used to come out there when you had a job out there, Tom's Roadhouse? I said, yeah, that's a long time ago, 1920 then, and then I went to work with, with Buzzy Williams and Charlie Fishbein, I worked at the Arcadia Ballroom, that was ballroom dancing, and that incidentally became the first, after about a year after we left, it became the first Nicola dance hall in town. Then I went to work with, or I went to work with the Buzzy and Charlie at the Cadillac, I stayed all the time with them, there were changes made in between, I stayed with them at the Cadillac, then I went to Bucktown, Joe Julien's with them, then I went to Tom Anderson's on Rampart between Canal and Iverville, they had two Tom Anderson's, you know, one was on the corner of Basin and Iverville, then the other Tom Anderson, you know, the Tom Anderson place, but on Rampart between Canal and Iverville, then I went to the La Vida. Oh, I got married when we were working at the Tom Anderson, and the funny thing, well of course in them days they used to feed you the musicians, you know, of course like, we'd always have, like two would go at a time, you know, I'd always had music on the stand there, and the cook at Tom Anderson, she said to me, she said, how are you getting married? I said, yeah. I said, well it's not going to be a big wedding, I told her. She said, well where's it going to be? I said, St. Joseph Church. She said, well I'll tell you, she said, there might not be anybody else there, she said, but I'll be there, the cook said. Sure enough, she was there. Then I worked at La Vida, I went to the La Vida with them, and of course we were in the music business, and I was married too, and my wife was scared to stay up at the store at night, don't blame her, stay upstairs, you know. So I used to have to take her home to her mother's every night and sleep. So I played, stayed there up, well into 1924, and then a friend of mine, I left my drums over there for him, I said, I'm going to leave the job, I just gave my two weeks notice and I said, if you want, I said, you can take the job, I said, I know you'll be able to stay on the job with him, I said, use my drums as long as you want. So he went over there and he showed that he was quite good by it for quite a while. And I didn't play too much then, I played just, hmm, just once in a while or something like that, you know, spots, maybe a parade or something. And I didn't start playing again until 1929, then when I went to work at Stale at the place called the College on Ramport between Canal and, out between Conti and Biennual there. And then of course, I, oh yeah, in the 30s, I believe I went down and played with the Peep of Cope, his band down in the Green Mill, just for a week, I didn't want to really, I didn't want to play too much anymore after
that, I really wanted to, well in, well in 24 and 25, even though I had my store, I worked

for the Count Van Aachen and the company too. And I didn't know that they were doing it, of course the fellow that was the owner of the store, he used to be around the store at night after it was cold, always come up and see me and I would tell. And he said to me, you know, he said, man, I'm not selling any drums, he said, man, I have a tough time, he said, why don't you come down and sell some drums and some instruments for me, he said, I'll make it worth your while. So I said, okay, I said, I'll do that, I told him, I asked my wife, we all right, she said, yeah. And I went over there, and after I was over there about a year, he said to me, he said, the Count Company wants you to open up a store in Shreeport, I said, well, I'm sorry I can't make that. But I did very well at the place. I prayed like, parades, like I played maybe on a spot job once in a while like that somewhere. But in 29, into 30, I played quite a bit then. And then after that I played like, I played the Rex Parades, I played the Feynman Day Parades, and I played, well, in Biloxi and Gratner and West W- and, you know, West W- I played some of that too. And I used to play the St. Rosalie Parade, you know, a few things, play Spock now and then. But I did that up until about 1947, until I had my first operation, and that was just about the animal playing days. Or around 48, when jazz, see jazz revised, revived itself. Well, Tom Brown used to come around, Happy Shillin, and Johnny Lala. Well, I had worked with, you see, there's a lot of these bands I worked with too, you know, during my days, way back there, like, Charlie Dykeman's band, Borda's band, Charlie Borda, Don Chase, Johnny Batusa, George Shillin. Oh, I used to play with George Shillin when he had, I didn't work too long on these things. We used to play at the Moose home on Saturday nights, and we used to have the bally hole from the Royalton Canal, Bourbon and Canal, Dolphin and Canal, and then Ramport Canal, and then we'd walk back to the home, you know. And then, you ever stood up playing drums? Geez, that's the hardest thing in the world to do. And that, yeah.
What Shillin is that? George Happy.

That's Happy, not his son. Oh, no, no, well, this is a long time ago. Yeah. And, yeah, I worked there. Yeah, he had, and then of course when Happy, a lot of times Happy Shillin used to get two jobs, and Johnny Lollard, Johnny was the fellow who played the jazz, the hornet, you know, and he also played a little piano, too cool to think. And when he got two jobs, of course this was, if I wasn't working, of course in the daytime I couldn't make them, and picnics and things like that. Well I used to play with the band, you know, Johnny Lollard. That was one of my biggest boosters, Johnny Lollard. He, you know, in this music business you gotta have boosters, you gotta have guys to talk, see. And he was one of my good talkers. I was, he brought some fellas from, when I was working at the Cadillac, he brought some fellas from St. Louis. They came down to hear me play, and they went to go join a band in St. Louis. And, well, Rapp, Rapp came back to town too long, and I'm 23, I believe, and he spoke to me about going to Chicago, and I told him, I said, man, he said, how much are you making there? I told him how much I was making. It was the best job in town, the theater then. Best extra money. Well, Charlie always paid over the scale, always paid me over the scale, and I guess he paid all the other guys too, I don't know how much he ever paid the other guys, but he was the best lead out. I made more money with Charlie Fishbaum and Buzzie Williams than with any other bands. And, when I worked down at Cadillac, oh gee, the Tips was terrific down there, a lot of days, man, I'm telling you, he'd be surprised. We played for entertainers, you know, we had entertainers, you know, and Buzzie Williams was one of the greatest piano players for entertainers. Man, I'm telling you, he could play in between the keys. Sometimes the girls would get on the floor and he'd sing out his joint or something, and he'd say, how'd I do it buddy? He'd say, oh you did fine honey, you know, we're making that money, you know, and it was all. But, yeah, we, and then, or, the Vida last, yeah, we had a Hawaiian, Hawaiian girl dancing, we had a Hawaiian outfit out there too that we played for, I moved into the Vida too, yeah, they were pretty good. But most of them had like entertainers, like girls singers, you know, fellas singing, you know, something like that. But we, I did pretty good with, I did pretty good with, I liked to play with Charlie and Bunny, but Bunny was great. And I never heard anybody any, any fine. And of course a lot of guys played good now, but to me, he was very, piano for entertainers, he was terrific. And he played pretty good dance piano too now. Dan Kosauer was in the music business, that was a big thing for us. And so many fellas came around, you know, Eddie Milliman, he was a young fella. Oh, funny thing, talking about Johnny Batusi's band, you see, Johnny Batusi had a band in New Orleans before he went to, along the Gulf Coast. Yeah. Well, Ellis Stratikas is playing, Ellis was living in Gulfport at this time, I believe his dad had a confectionary or something over there. Well anyway, when Ellis was playing with Johnny, that, he was living, you know, Johnny had bands in the Gulf Coast, and Johnny had a candy store and his old ice cream right on the street going to the beach, him on your mama, right? So, yeah.
I was going to ask you, it had Imperial Jazz on the drum, in that picture of Johnny Batusi's band? Yeah. And Ellis is playing the drums, Ellis Stratikas.
That's what they tell me, well that's Johnny, Johnny's put the names on there, see.
Oh yeah, I see. Yeah, Johnny put the names on there.
And Joe Loicano Trombone.
Joe Loicano Trombone. And Henry Lopo said, said, on them.
Yeah, yeah.
And Henry, how do you pronounce his name? Harry Tarzan, T-A-U-C-I-N. Harry Tarzan. Harry Tarzan. Yeah, he played good clarinet, played real good clarinet. And you knew him, huh?

Oh yes, oh, well played a little bit. I know almost nothing about him. Well, Harry Tarzan played, before I went out to the, uh, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, before I played before I had a band out at the, uh, Roadhouse out there, I heard him playing with a band and I think he was playing with- Jules Cherzaud was playing piano. I think Mary Brunesse was playing cornet in them days, Harry Tarzan clarinet. And I think it was George Treey on drums, played fine drums. one of my dad's students who played fine. He played in the theaters too, he played in the theater. But I remember they played out there sometime there and Harry taught them play. Yeah, Harry played good clarinet and he had a band over in Block City, I don't remember. A fellow by the name of Dick Pitcher used to play cornet with him. I don't know him. Oh, none of the guys know him pretty well, but he played some new arms here. And Jeff Reddick's brother played piano with him, Johnny Reddick, Harry, Luke Dubas, I believe his folks was in the oyster business over there, you know. Yeah, I think he played drums. He had a five piece band. He was playing trombone. His sister was over
there and I read or heard somewhere that there was a fellow named Burt and he had the Five

Aces Down from Chicago. Do you know that? Oh man, I heard that band play. That's the band that I'm telling you about that when Boynie and I went over there they had some differences with the band. Yeah. Uh, Foxy Marriott, let's see if I can tell you the name of the piano player. Jesus, I believe, what was his name now? Gee whiz. Uh, Bob Sackerman played saxophone. Oh yeah, I met his niece. Well, Bob Sackerman played saxophone and I played with Bob later on when he came to New Orleans. He came to New Orleans to live. And I played in bands with Bob Sackerman. But Bob played saxophone. Let's see now. Oh, Jimmy Boyle, a fellow that was a former student of my dad's, he played in the Liberty Theater and he was working
with them. They had Foxy Marriott I believe was one of the guys' names. Who was the drummer?
Bert Lilly was the corner player's name I believe. Bert Lilly. Bert Lilly. And a fellow by the name of Arnold Johnson or something like that. Yeah. John Johnson played piano I think. Yeah, well,
Conquer Johnny Lawler used to play with him. Who? Johnny Lawler used to play with him in Chicago, I think, Conquer Johnson. Well, you know, Johnny Lawler told me about him years ago.

Yeah, well, anyway, I think he was playing piano. But they had, well, I tell you, the guy on that saxophone was terrific. Man, that guy could play some saxophone. He played more like, yeah, that's the fella, that's the one band, they were over there when Barney and I went over and played with Charlie because they had some kind of a difference. And we stood over, we stood over, Dan and I, I don't know, where was playing carnet. Well, anyway, Dan and I stood over that night. We had heard somebody had said how good this saxophone player played. Dan, you see, Dan was Fazola's first teacher. Mm-hmm. Faz started off on a saxophone, a brass saxophone. Dan, he didn't like the sound of the sax. Faz never liked the sound of a saxophone. Yeah. And then he, uh, you see, Faz at one time played the band system clarinet. Then he broke a key or something on the clarinet. Yes. And, uh, I don't know, I can't tell you where he bought it because he didn't buy it from me anyway, but this is way back in a long time when he was young. And, uh, but they sound, I think they sent the wrong key in or something and then it, then he picked up an Albert system clarinet. And I think it was a Pendulum or Albert system clarinet. And they found out you got that big sound out of it, see. Yeah. Out of the Albert. And he goes, and then he starts using that and, uh, well, that's what he used, you know. He used Albert system. And I think, uh, I think he studied with both of them. I think he started with, uh, Gene Parking on the main system and then later I think with, uh, with, uh, Santo Giuffre, I think. Because, oh, I remember he talked about Santo Giuffre. He told me that Santo Giuffre had made, had refaced a mouthpiece for him. Well, Santo Giuffre used to play in the Tulane Theater with my, when my dad played there, Santo Giuffre, right back. In fact, Santo Giuffre is the man that learned my mother how to cook, uh, Italian dishes. Oh, awesome. Oh, yes. He was, so, and it was great. Is that from uptown, Santo Giuffre? Uh, Santo Giuffre at this time was living on Galvis,
I think between, uh, Berks and Palmyra. Now, the Six and Magazine bunch, that was the Cassards from up there.

Yes, sir. I see. Yeah, yeah. And Santo Giuffre, yeah, and he was telling me about some fella, I used to always tell him, I'd say, Father, never let them fellas put any heat on your mouthpiece. Uh-huh. And he said that he was in the jam one night, that's one day or something, he had to go and work, and he said the fella put the car and put the heat on, he said never could get any sound out of that particular mouthpiece. And he said that, he really told me that was one of the finest mouthpieces he has ever had. He said it was a great mouthpiece. And that one was a good, uh, oh man, that guy could play. Yeah, we worked, I worked with him with, uh, with Steele. We played jobs there with Steele around 29. And man, that guy could play. Oh man, he got, he, he died fairly young, huh? Yeah. Uh, I could, I'm pretty good. Well anyway, talking about Bob, man, I don't know, you see in them days, because most guys that played saxophone around the early 20s, they got a nanny-goose type of sound, you know, crying type. Lester Nelson, did you ever meet Lester Nelson? Never did, never did. Oh lord, you talk about good, tenor, one of the greatest. Well anyway, Lester, Lester used to laugh at some of these guys, he said to me, he said so-and-so and he's crying saxophone, I'm not going to mention the guys he used to tell, he said man, so-and-so. And, but Bob, Bob could, I tell you, I never heard at that time, of course you know, it's advanced so far, now fast, you know, these guys make monkeys jump off of the horns, you know. But in them days, he got such a fine sound. I mean a fine sound, I tell you, I never heard of anybody get a sound out of a saxophone like Bob Zagerman did. That's funny, I just happened to meet his
relative on Mardi Gras Day from up around Chicago, that area. I don't remember the exact time.

Well I believe his brother was the leader of a theater orchestra in Chicago. Could have been. Somebody had told me that, I don't remember Bob saying anything about it, but somebody told me that he was, of course, was a leader, and somebody told me that's when he went up to the show up in Chicago, he worked in the theater up there. Now that, of course, that's all hearsay stuff, I never heard from Bob, I never seen him, of course, after he left New Orleans, but he got great, great.
He still has relatives in town.
Yeah.
His family, yeah.

Oh wait, let's see a funny thing now. I think that was his son. Hal, didn't he have a son that played something? Bob Zagerman. I don't really know. Gee whiz. I'm trying to think of somebody that used to come around the store that used to talk about him. And I thought it was...
There's very few people that would remember him now, because that's a long time ago, and he wasn't yet.
Well, he left here around 1930, I imagine, around that time.
Probably still.
So that's over 40, it's almost 50.
He died fairly soon, I think.
Yeah, right after that he died, he sure did.
And, oh, back to the White City. Where did the Pelicans play?

The Pelicans played on Cleveland and Counting Avenue, around that way somewhere. They had the ballpark there. Yeah. And of course later on they moved to, you know, where they, you know, they're fresh out there on Counting and Tulane.
Yes. So, the White City is, was not the same place where they played. I mean, it's, later on, Pelican Stadium was right near there, huh?
Well, it was on Cleveland Avenue.
Yeah, but then later on they moved to Tulane and Carrollton.
Yes, that's right.
And where was White City? Which corner was it on?

Man, it's been so long. Yeah, well I can look it up. It was on, anyway, it was on Counting and Tulane because we used, I used to go out there with my dad and all, you know, and we, I was always... Did you play for the ball games or not? No, not, oh, did he play for the ball? Yeah, he played once for Heinemann Park with, with Charlie Bowler had a band out there for years. And my dad played at the racetrack also with Charles Bowler too, Charles had a, and I played the, I played the political, Dally Hoos with Charles Bowler, and I played the parades with Charles Bowler. And I also played with Charles Bowler out at Spanish Ford, I believe I forgot to tell you that. Yeah, I played with Charles Bowler when he had a band out at Spanish Ford, that's true, sure did. And Dan's Pavilion out there every night, you know.
And you played for funerals too, you said?

Oh yeah, I played for funerals when I was real young over in Gretna. You see, years ago, the Musicians Union, now this wasn't for no musician, this one, or these D's that I played, but the musicians used to furnish a ten piece band when a member died, and the band used to play at the church. And the last time that I remember that they had a band was when Emile Stein had died, and it seemed like to me, Emile must have been living on Arch Street or something, it was a church down around, somewhere around in this section, maybe a little further in town. And I remember when Emile died, and that's about the last time that I remember, you know, you could request a band, and they'd play like, you know, some kind of a hymn or any way, you know, any hymn you want to play.
Well, in Gretna now, who would that be for?
Well, an individual. I mean, I wouldn't know who it was Gretna.
It wouldn't be a member of an organization?
Oh gee, that's so long ago, that's go back when I was fourteen, fifteen years.
Well, Jack Lane used to tell me about playing for funerals.

Yeah, gee, I'm trying to think of who I played with over there for them. In fact, the musician used to talk about some musician that's, they used to say, he used to get a lot of the funerals way back, he used to say he used to sit on the step and wait for the man to die to get the job, you know. You know what I mean? That's what they, I was just saying, you know. Yeah. Well, I felt a name, I remember, I knew the fellow too, but an older musician, see. But yes, I played some, when I was real young over there in Gretna. Now, I don't remember too much about him. I remember playing, walking to the cemetery with him. And, oh, Dick, I played so many things, it's really good. But, to goodness, unless there's something that would happen that I'd remember, it's really hard, you see.
Well, Jack Lane would talk about the Owls and Davy Crockett, those different firemen's things and all that sort of stuff.
But I really couldn't tell you, I don't remember whether it was, it must have been an organization, because that's about the only one that it would be for.
Yeah, I would think so.

But that's when I was really young, so young then when I played, that kind of thing. Like political meetings, I used to play political meetings with bands, you know. And I was, like I say, I was pretty lucky in the early days, because I could play with the union and non-union musicians, which was really good for me.
When you were under age.
Yeah, my dad said after I got eighteen, well, before I got eighteen I had to join them. Oh, when I joined a musician, you had to pass the test.
I see.

And after the Jazz Band, the original Dixieland Jazz Band made these recordings, then he eliminated the test, see, and anybody could come in then, you see. No, the musicians union in them days, those fellas were all artists, you know. It was a different breed, different breed of musicians, and a happy-go-lucky type, you know. And they were serious musicians, very serious. And like the other guys, you know, they were all, they had a lot of bands that played good, you know, of course, talk about, well, Jules played with one of Jack Lane's bands too, you see. Jules Casanoff. My uncle, rather. And, well, of course, around, you see, he didn't have bands when I was really playing real good then, at that time, because you never heard of Jules. And, you know, he might have played up until around, maybe, 1970 or 18, but I'll tell you, oh, he was a very, very good friend of my dad's. Yes. And, of course, his son, Alfred, was a very good friend of mine. Yes. Alfred used to have bands around too. The last time I saw Alfred, he was playing bass drum with the police band, but he played cornet, and I believe he played maybe upright, something else, one of his days. But, you see, everybody talked about bands in them days as ragtime. Yes. And, they really didn't start to talk about jazz until after the original Dixieland band made the first recordings. Then jazz became, you know, people start, they got jazz minded then. See, they would start talking about jazz. Nobody, now the fellas that they used to talk about, most of the old times would talk about, they'd say, who was the originator of jazz? Well, who was the originator of jazz? Some fellas would say Stair Brad. Some fellas would say Johnny Hunter, Johnny Stein, you know, Johnny Hunter. Johnny Stein, some would say Johnny Stein, some would say Johnny, well, you know about Johnny Hunter then. And some would say, the original Dixieland band. They never would say anything but the original Dixieland band. They didn't point out any individual. And Tom Brown. Now the blacks couldn't care less who was the originator of jazz. They never even, none of them ever discussed it. They didn't, they didn't give it even thought. Really, truthfully. They never gave it a thought about who originated jazz. And those were the fellas that they really, those were the bands that they taught. Of course they said the original Dixieland band and they never said nobody in the band. Now, if Nick LaRocca would have had Nick LaRocca and the original Dixieland jazz band, Nick LaRocca would have probably got an awful lot of publicity out of that thing, eh? But he didn't, he didn't use the name, it was just sort of more or less like you might say a co-op deal or something. And but he, and of course like I say, he was the leader of the band, but nobody ever said, when they talked about the band, they said the original Dixieland jazz band. They never said Nick LaRocca or LaRocca. Of course, my favorite was Lowry Shields. I liked the style of the Clannes. I always liked Clannes playing. I thought Clannes playing gave a New Orleans band that New Orleans sound. Because most of the bands you heard way back, they were plenty brassy, loud. But I tell you, now here's one thing too, I've got to tell you this. No matter how bad a black band sounded, it was always danceable. I don't care, they always had something about it. And you know for years, I made a study of that, and I used to listen to the guys come around the store and play, you know. And I found out one thing, you know what it was? Every, almost every one of the old timers that I knew, they all played rhythm on their instruments. They played rhythm. They didn't need no drums. They didn't know they were band-job players, they didn't need a piano player. I used to have them come around there and play around there for hours. Sometime, man, they, you see my, my style was always hot in the summer and cold in the winter. It was air-conditioned, you know. Hot in the summer and cold in the winter, you know. Man, they said to me, man, this is your, and man, somebody would be playing, I said, they'd have, their shirts would be ringing wet. And they'd say to me, man, you know, I'm getting ready to go on the job. And he said, man, look at my shirt, they'd be playing for two or three hours. Just standing up there by themselves playing. Great. But that's one thing. No matter how bad the band sound, it was danceable. But when you got a, tell you, when you got a bad white band now, it was kind of bad. It was kind of bad. But they all more or less, like I said, the old timers all played rhythm on the instruments. It's true. Yeah. And I sure used to have a lot of fun with a mountaineer. Another, another old, old-time musician used to visit me quite a bit was Red Island's daddy. He used to live over the river, you know, and he used to, once or never, a couple of months, he'd come over and spend about an hour just talking about music, you know, musicians and things like that. But they never did say about how great guys played. Never. No, but they didn't care. Eh, they didn't care. They couldn't care less who did this or who did that. All they wanted to do was to play that music. And I think one thought he played just as good as the others was. I used to get a big kick out of Peter Davis, you know, the one that played and taught Louie. He used to hang around the store quite a bit. And somebody wrote a book, you see, in them days Louie was out of the Jones home out there, you know. And Peter Davis was working out there too, and he was teaching the band too, see. And somebody wrote a book and it said that Jones taught Louie how to play the cornet, see. And Manny would come around the store and he said, man, he'd get so mad about that. He said, you know, he said, Joan, they never taught Louie. And, you know, and some fellas, sometime when he'd be around, he'd say, man, I see where Jones started, man. He'd get him all around. Peter was kind of tall and skinny, you know. But, yeah, I used to have him around there quite a bit now. We'd say, well, have fun that one. Them guys all, all like to play that music.
Louie Armstrong and all these different musicians, but did you ever play the banjo? I know you used to sell banjo mutes. They talk about that. Yeah. You kept all different kind of accessories, huh?
In my store you could get anything you wanted, see. You see, Dick, here's the dip. You got this on and on?
It's on.

It is. Dick, you see, this is the thing. I was a musician. I come from musical families from way back, see. You get kind of, you don't look for the dollar sign. All right. Let's see. Now, yeah, I'm trying to think of, oh gee, well, you see. Think of some of them guys, man. Gee whiz. Yeah, there was a, well, we used to call this a tone control, a tone control, see. And you could raise it, you know, a lot closer you'd put it to the band, the bridge, you know, the moment before the sound would get. Oh, what's the fella's name that used to come on then and I used to have to run him out there and taking his hat off all the time when he was coming there, the banjo player.
Oh, not the one that used to go on up about reeds.

Oh, no, that was John Casimir. Funny thing talking about John Casimir. You know John Casimir. Sure. John Casimir used to use plastic reeds, see. And no matter, any reed I ever got, I used to have to have, I had a special reed, not a special reed, but a reed cutter just for him, for his reeds, see. I used to have to always cut, he'd say to me, they won't play unless you cut part of that reed off for me. Come on, John Casimir. And he called up my wife and said, well, you know, she'd call him and tell him when I got his reeds in or something like that. But any kind of a set, you name it, we had it. We had anything for instruments. Now I remember when John Schaaf was taken from, oh that's the guy I first sent John in there, played with George E. Lewis, the banjo player. Lawrence Moreira. Lawrence Moreira. Yeah. Lawrence Moreira used to send a lot of fellas over for those tone controls, you know. And that's the first time I met John Schaaf when he was real young, you know. And of course John and we were very, very friendly all the way, you know.
And Billy Huntington was another pupil of his.

Billy Huntington, yeah, Billy. Well, uh. Bill he is. Yeah, Bill Huntington. Yeah, Bill Huntington. Well, his dad used to come around quite a bit. His dad played violin, see. His dad used to come around with Bill. Bill was just, you know, young. In fact, a lot of like, what you call him now, Dr. John. When he was little, his dad used to bring him around. Yeah. But getting back to Johnny Petusi's band, I wanted to tell you this too. Eddie Miller's dad, you know, Eddie Miller's dad and I were very, very good friends too. Well Eddie as a kid, he would hang around and start to. I had Eddie playing on the Strand Theater one day when he was just about, I guess twelve years old. And with a band, you know, made him get out and front blow. He could, he always could play good too, Eddie. Even with a kid, like Pete Fontaine, same thing. But Eddie Miller's daddy used to dance to Johnny Petusi's band when Johnny had bands in New Orleans. And Pete Fontaine's dad used to dance to Johnny Petusi's music when Johnny Petusi had bands in Biloxi. Now both of these fellas, both of these men told me this. And Eddie Miller's dad used to always say to me, he said, there's one song that Johnny Petusi used to play, he said, I always, man, I always liked that song. It was Love Me Lou. And I used to tell him, you see every time Johnny Petusi came to town, he came to see me. Am I? Always. Every time he came to town, he'd come to see me. And Johnny and I were very good friends too.
Go ahead. No, you're good. Tell me. I was just wondering about Eddie Miller's instrument then. What did he play when you first knew him?

Clownet. Eddie Miller played with a little band. I'll tell you who the band was. It was Eddie Miller, Lloyd Miller played drums, Benny Miller played banjo, and a fella by the name of Irwin Carroll played cornet. And they used to call him Carroll Miller. But none of these three millers were related. They used to play with little ball games and little different things like that, see. And it'd all be around the store all the time, you know. And that's what Eddie's first instrument. And Eddie played fine. I used to have Eddie listening to Leon Rapolo, the great rap, record all the time, see. When they made the record with the New Orleans Rhythm King. Men had ever been stood there for hours and hours, you know, just playing on the record. Same thing like, what Pete, with Foz's record, see. Well, Rapolo, rap, you know. And Eddie Miller always thought that rap was one of the greatest kind of phrase of all time. And I guess, maybe, uh, uh, Pete thinks that, uh, Irwin Cazola was one of the greatest, you know. And Foz was one of the greatest kind of phrase I've ever heard. I swear on it after hearing. He was great. Oh, he was great. And he wasn't swell headed though, did he? No. And he didn't like anyone that was swell headed. Man, you'd be surprised. He didn't like anyone that had the swell head. And his brother, Louie, you know, Louis Gustavnik. Yeah. Anyway, Louis used to have good bands, society type of bands, real good bands, you know. Yeah. And Bobbie, well, you know, Louie didn't live too long after Irvin died. Too long, uh-uh. And I think more or less he may have grieved on it because he loved, he loved Irvin, you know. Yeah. Well, you see, you say, well, I had fun, Irvin. Sometimes he'd be in there, I'd be, man, sometimes he'd bring around the flute and he'd play flute, you know. Maybe I'd put a pad or two on the flute or something, he'd play flute. Sometimes he'd be around there with the client at the sax. He was always, he played, he didn't like to play the sax, but he always, the sound. He'd say to me, man, that C on that horn is flat, you know what I mean? And I'd cut the key a little bit and raise it up, you know what I mean? And say, yeah, yeah, sure. But he, wonderful ear. Oh, Lord. And as a young kid he was great on, the fellas used to talk how great he was on transpositions. He could take any parts and play them on the clarinet, see, the guy was a marvelous musician. And he used to tell me all the time, he used to practice a lot of chords on the piano. That explains all that. That's what he told me, he said, I used to practice a lot of chords on the piano. But we used to have a lot of fun with him. I'd always be in there starting time and he'd say to me, pal, man, you know something? I got meat out in the car, it'd be in July or August, you know, and he said, man, he said, the sun is all beating down on that meat. He said, by the time I get home, it'll be rotten. But he was a great guy and we liked him very, very much, I tell you. He started an awful lot of them. But almost all the musicians, you see, when you're a musician, you cater to musicians, you see. When I went in business, you see, you know what all the musicians told me? You'll never make any money fooling around with musicians. Now sometimes the boys would come around there and you know where they'd be? They'd come around the corner, you know where they'd be? They'd be on the outside there knitting. And they'd say, they'd come in and say, I know he's going to be here almost a whole day with you, so I brought my knitting along and he'd sit out in the car. Man, we always had, we didn't make much money, but boy, we used to have a lot of fun, you know, that was a big thing. But there was always a musician there talking music, see, and that was a big thing for them, you know. Done a lot of, and a lot of kids, young kids used to come around there, man, they'd have them out wide open, listen to them fellas, you know. And some of them saxophone players said to me, man, I heard that guy play. He said, man, how'd you get that growling sound out of that saxophone? There used to be a fellow around here, my name was Sam Lee, man, he played great. Got that growling sound, man, you know. And one day, we'd be around the store there, oh, he had said to me, he said, you know, he said, Ms. Peters, I can buy a recording machine. He said he got in the pawn shop, he said, man, real cheap. I said, how are you talking, man? I said, man, gee, that's not too expensive. I said, man, and you, Harrison Barrett, I don't know if you knew Harrison Barrett played guitar, banjo, banjo. Well, he was, he's related to Fats Domino, I mean, anyway. Well, anyway, Harrison, I said, well, you know, well, him and Harrison, I believe it was related to something. I said, man, Harrison played a banjo, a guitar. I said, man, I said, you were the saxophonist, you'd go around these clubs all around these ballrooms and all, and take them people and make money. So, he bought the machine anyway, and funny thing, I used to send him the recal-, the blanks, you know, for the machine. I used to have the auto, you know, blanks for it for him. So, well, and he said to me, he said, you know, he said, man, he said, you told me, he said, I was going to make money off of that thing. He said, well, all that thing you've ever done has cost me money. He said, my wife has got so many friends, he said, she said, Sam, recal her. He said, but I don't get no money out of it, he said. And, man, he used to laugh about that. So, one day, I had a machine around there, and he was playing sax, and I was, had a tom-tom, you know, beating on a tom-tom on the big tom. And, man, he said, you know something, he said, man, he said, while we're playing there, he said, I'm recording it, and he played it back, see. And, he said to me, he said, oh, at this time, he was playing at the powder club, Papa, well, Oscar Celestine, you know, Oscar was playing the band, and he said to me, he said, I'm working on a powder club. He said, Papa heats them up, and he said, I cooled them off. They used to advertise them, it was a whole lot of old Sam, see. And, lad, so he saw Shoggy, he said, say, Mr. Shoggy, he said, say, Mr. Shoggy, you know something, he said, me and Mr. Pete, he said, we made us a twosome racket, a twosome. And, lad, boy, used to get a kick out of that.
He's on the west coast now.

Yeah, well, he went to California, yeah, I think his boy went out there too, his boy was playing drums. But, talking about drumming, I'm going to tell you something, because, you know, I used to have an awful lot of drummers around there.
But, one of the finest drummers I've ever had around here, this fella incidentally was black, on Craven Street.

This fella used to, when he'd go on a job, this is the truth, he used to have a second line following him. Kids, see, second line. So, he used to come around the store all the time, and him and I would get on the drums, you know what I mean. And, one night he played a job, and after the job where he was living, he went down to the corner to get a bottle of pop. Wasn't no drinking fella, pop now, root beer or something. And while he's in there, some fella comes in there and kills him. And he's on the ground, and it's not, this is hearsay, what I'm going to tell you now about this, because the kids are the ones coming around and telling me about it. He said, man, your friend got killed. He's killed, I said, and he said, the fella turned him over and he said, man, I killed the wrong man.
Gee.

That fella was the American, one of the finest drummers I have ever heard, white or black, I'm telling you the truth. The guy was great. Man, man, I said, look at this boy, ain't that a shame? But that's what they were telling me. Now, he never came around the store anymore after that, so it had to be true.
What was his name?
Oh, Lord, that's, he's in the 30's, man. That's, I don't even, you know.
Yeah, that slips your mind.
Man, I tell you, you forget so many kids, you know, so many kids around, you know.
And he was just a youngster.

Well, I'd say he was about 18, 19 maybe. He played good. Oh, he played so good. He had a second line. This kid just, every time he played, man, they'd all be with him, way to go and see him, stand outside and hear him play. The guy was great. But, man, I remember this fellow that used to play with the Ringling Brothers show, Ray Floyd. I don't guess you ever met Ray Floyd, did you?
No, never did.

Anyway, Ray, Ray used to be around the store quite a bit, too. And Ray, Ray used to tell me, he said, man, he used to, oh, he's going to write some drum company and tell him, you know, of course, we know all the drum companies, you know, the fellow that's in them. He said, I'm right so-and-so. He said, and George Ware, somebody else said, and Ray said, man, they come in here to buy a pair of drumsticks and you give them a free drum lesson, he used to say, you know, laugh. I said, well, I guess that's it, man. One day, one night he was around there, man, and he used to laugh, man. He'd be sitting out there in the front laughing, you know, I'd be in the back there, you know. And one day, one evening I had a fellow in there, he never did play bass drum in a parade, see, and he always wanted to play bass drum in a parade. And he never knew where to come in, you know, after the roll off, you know. So, man, I was back there with him, and boy, he said to me, and he's out in front, man, I'm telling you, he's laughing out loud, you know. And he says to me, he says, man, he says, can you get that? He says, what do you know about that? He says, the guy went to play bass drum in a parade, you know. And he's getting a big kick out of that because the guy went to play bass drum, he wants to know where to come in on the roll off, you know. Yeah, we had so many guys, but the music game was great because, I mean, you met so many fellas and you knew so many fellas, you know.
Oh, you were talking about Tony Giardino? Now, who started with Tony? He did.
Hal started playing with Tony Giardino, he was really young. I guess you must have been about 14, 15, isn't he?
When I was in Peter's high school at him, like 1940, 1941, before I graduated from high school. Played at Feynman's Hall in West Wigo.
I never heard him there, but I used to hear him out at Happy Landing. I think it was at Happy Landing.
Oh, yeah, he sure did play. Was his wife playing piano with him? Yes. His wife died. What was that, did that guy have played with him?
That must have been in the early 50s.
Oh, that was it. That was it. That was it. That's the name of the guy that you played with him because, let's see.
I went into service in 1943 and got out in 1946.
Yeah, Charlie Cusack was playing drums with him. Remember Charlie, you met Charlie Cusack? Charlie was playing drums with him.
No, I don't remember. Oh, what was the old bass player? Roscoe Legnan, I believe, used to play bass. Yeah.
Was Roscoe Legnan playing with him? I believe so.
I don't know what you're talking about. I don't know. I don't remember. I knew a guy named Larry Labatt. I know a guy named Larry Labatt that used to play trumpet with him.
But Labatt used to go to school with George at Warren Easton.
Oh, you mean tall, tongue-tall, working for the city or something?
Yeah, he's still working for the city.
Yeah, because of the cameras or something, wasn't he? He went to Warren Easton with my brother.
He and his wife like to walk. And so I see him all the time. I sit on the way of the car.
We haven't seen him in years.
As a matter of fact, I ran across him not too long ago playing music one night at a wedding or something. Haven't seen him in years. I believe he lived around the French Quarter or something.
Yeah, I think it was around the French Quarter.

Yeah, Tony Jardina was a real fine clarinet. Oh yeah. You ought to hear this guy play clarinet. That was the first, I guess, real professional band I'd ever played with. I was only about 14, 15 years old.
Yeah, Tony made a couple of them parades with us over in the Bronx or two of them Finman Day parades.
Well, there's so many people like that that have forgotten. Like you were talking about Ricky Tom. I don't even know where he was from.
Well, from New Orleans as long as I know him. He played with Papa Lane way back too, Ricky.
And Melvin Berry, that was another one that I hear people talk about.
Well, Mel Berry played with, Mel Berry played with Charlie and I when, I bet, Carlton, just at the time, I'm telling you that the Dixieland band.
Charlie Fishbrunner.

Yeah. Well, Mel Berry was playing in the Palisade at this time, see, when, you know, yeah. Mel, let's see, we had a combination, let's see, we had Joe Martinez on piano, rather, Charlie, this was his band. Joe Martinez on piano. We had Frank Portune on clarinet. He went out to California too. Melvin Berry on trombone, Charlie Fishbrunner myself. No corner, foul and fiddling. Oh, talking about Dave Perkins. You knew Dave Perkins? Oh, no, you didn't meet Dave.
Oh, Dave was dead. No, he was dead. He died a few years ago.

Well, talking about Dave Perkins, you see, I used to make quite a few jobs, you know, in and around town, out of town too. And sometimes I couldn't make the job with him, see, and he'd say to me, come and say to me, see, man, he said, you know, you're playing with, all you're doing is playing with them Sweet Marie bands, he used to call them, band with them fiddles in it, see. Sweet Marie bands. Sweet Marie bands, see. And I used to tell him, I said, well, Dave, I said, man, I said, those are the fellas that are working, see. A lot of the fiddle players, you know what I mean, in them days, like Charlie and Max Fink and Rainey Solomon and Joe Calro, all them guys were playing, you know, all fiddle men, you know what I mean? And they got jobs, and they got study jobs most of them too, you know what I mean? The other guys were playing these once in a while jobs, you know? And I had to make money, I couldn't just play them once. And it was, you know, New Orleans was really a big, like a big Saturday night deal, you know what I mean? The fellas played on Saturday nights, and then during the summertime they played picnics out of different places. But it wasn't like it is now, and during the Lent time the only time the bands played most of them was on St. Joseph's night. People really didn't go to dances, you know, but now they go any time, any time to dances. But, and then, like I said, of course, there wasn't too many clubs around in them days too, you know, there wasn't too many clubs.
And you had pianists around that were playing?
Who's that?
You had piano players.
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
There were some of them that played solo, you're talking about black key piano players.

Well, no, they could tune the piano, you know, tune the piano, natural keys, you know, you can tune the piano that way too. Oh, I see. You know, instead of playing C. You can just tune it down, I have to stand up. Playing C sharp, you're doing it in C, you know, you can raise it, lower it that half tone, you know. Yeah.
Yeah. So, the black key piano players, they could make it with bands if the piano was out of tune.

Oh man, you never heard anybody playing in your life, finding that fellow Leonard Bystoffer. I heard him playing with a little group, let's see, at the little club, when I was playing at the Cadillac. They were playing at the little club, let's see. Gee. I think he had himself on piano, Scaglione on clarinet, that's a fellow played good, he died young too. Scaglione on clarinet, they had, what did the fellow, you know, Leonard Mandeville, you know, friends of Oymans, you know. Oh, wow.
Or played drums.

Orzerman. Orzerman. Yeah, he played drums with them. Ernest Orzerman. Man, that tour was, it was terrific, man. And we used to, every now and then, we'd, at the Cadillac, you see, we used to get a lot of these, you know, people with money used to come down there. We made plenty of tips on that, it was a great job. And every now and then we'd get some rich guy come along, of course his chauffeur used to handle all the money, but man, he'd take us in his court, he'd take us over to like the little club and we'd have to play a couple of tunes over. Give us a ten dollar bill and we'd have to, you know, treat you to whatever you wanted and give you a ten dollar bill in the morning before you leave. And we went over there a couple of times, Charlie and I, and I guess probably the two, I don't remember. Well anyway, but man, that guy played some flying, oh, I heard him playing before that, I think I heard him playing at the Orchard Club too, on Conti and, when was it? It was in Conti and Bugandi, the Orchard Club, later it was Pete Harmon's place. And I heard him, man, that guy played some flying piano, gee whiz. I think him and Leonard, let's see, I think him and John, Johnny Vizdolfo, he was cousins some kind of one, I think they were, I'm not sure now. But man, he played some flying piano. They had a lot of guys play, they had a fellow by the name of Burgess, what was his first name, Louie Burgess' brother, who he played drums down the palace. Well the only one I ever heard was Joe Burgess. Joe Burgess. Oh man, Joe played fine too in them days. Joe, they wrote a lot of songs and all, Joe Burgess and some other guys around town, but I don't believe they ever made any money off of them.
Don't Leave Me Daddy was his hit. Don't Leave Me Daddy. But I still know, I still hear it.

But I think one of the tunes that was, what was, I'm sorry I made you cry, one of the guys, Plessy wrote that number I think. But I think he made a lot of money off, might have made money off of that one. But I don't know if any guys really made too much money. They had a show, a picture show, I believe they operated on Tulane, between Claiborne and Robison there years ago on the downtown side. Years ago, yeah. Man, there's so many musicians, boy, make their heads, huh?
Did we say anything about Bill Krieger when the machine was on? I know we were talking about him before.
Bill Krieger was one of the finest, you don't have it on now y'all?
Yeah, yeah, we have it on now.

Bill Krieger was one of the finest, clandest men I've ever heard. That's saying a lot now. Because I worked with Bill and when I had the band out at the roadhouse, the Thomas Roadhouse, he was working in Morton's out in Bucktown. That was up on the second floor, they had Morton's restaurant on the bottom dancing up top there. He was working up there with, let's see, I think he was working with Louis Frey was playing piano, Leslie Allen I believe was playing. Man, that's a guy who can play good fiddle. Nobody ever heard him talk too much, but he played good. Leslie Allen and I think either Emmett or Buck Rogers I think was playing drums and Bill. And Bill used to get, when somebody would come in and want to sit in, he'd come over and play with me over at the Thomas Roadhouse. He played great. He played great. He played fine. I liked the way he played. And funny thing, he could play good saxophone too. Not only played good clarinet, but played good saxophone.

I like what little I've heard of him on record. Oh man, he played good. He sure did. Well, was Don Peterson any kind of you, the super-comer player? No, no, no, no, no, no. Another name I came across in the Union book was Louis Peterson, but he worked for the Boot and Shoe Workers. He would come and plead that the musicians should buy Union shoes and Union boots.

Yeah, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Don Don played. Funny thing, I believe we had a brother by the name of Harold Peterson too. Yeah, we used to play with all those times. He sure did. We lived on Broadway and they lived on Broadway.
And he used to call out the mall. Oh yeah, that's huge. Did you ever go to the John Roof? Do you hear anybody up there? I don't know, Stratica.

Yeah, Stratica was about one of the few bands that I can remember that was up there. Yeah. Well, they recorded when they were up there. I don't remember anybody that had a band that played up there. I'm just trying to think. I think Stratica was the only band that played up there.
Did your sister ever make any records by the way? Lucille you mean? Yes.

Yeah, Bernie, no. You see, the first time when I was working out of the Bugtown, Leon Rapport was playing out there, and George E. Brunus, Joe Gowler was playing piano, myself. We used to have corner players. We never had any corner players. We used to have corner players just come in and sit in, you know, like Johnny Lala, Manny Blessie, Paul Merez, and a few guys. We only had trombone, clown and piano and drums, you know. That was one of the jobs, I mean, they really, it was supposed to be a union job and they wasn't any local either. In them days you could, if you couldn't get the union, you know, if you couldn't get anybody in union to play, you could get permission to use. Well anyway, one night out there we were playing and some fella used to come out there every night and listen to the band. One night he said to Leon Rapport, he said, say, man, I'd like to record the band, make a record of it. So Leon came to me this night and he said to me, say, how? He said, no money, no, you know, free alley. And I never played free alley at all. I'd have told my dad I'd make a record for free. So I told him, I said, he said, all you got to bring is a wood block and assemble. He said, well Rapport, you know, I said, I'm not that kind, I'm not a wood blocker. I said, you could get any of these guys that play wood boxers. I said, I'm a, I play on the side of the cell. I said, I'm a drummer. He said, so he wouldn't make the record, see. And him and I used to play the slot machine, we used to call it cow, we'd put in maybe about fifteen, twenty cents a piece of great liquor machine. And man, he wouldn't talk to me for quite a while about that. He was moody, wouldn't talk to me. So one night he said to me, he said, how? He said, let's play cow. First time he even said anything. So we put in maybe fifteen, twenty cents. And we hit the jackpot. And then, every now and then I can see him, counting them nickels, see. He had a hat there, and the money, he had that money and all in the hat, and he stood on the bench, and he was counting the nickels like that, putting them in the box. This is yours, this is mine, this is yours, this is mine. Maybe five hours we wanted, something like that. But yeah, he was a great client, I think. There's no question about that. He was one of the best, better ones that I heard. But Bill Krieger played great. I can't take anything away from him. I think he was one of the great clients then too. Of course there's other guys played. Johnny Provincana played pretty good client there. You never did hear Johnny. Never.
Johnny played.

In fact, Johnny used to come out when I worked out at the peak in Inman. Johnny used to come out every now and then play, you know, client. But he played good client there too. Johnny played real good.
Did you ever go to the Absent House to hear Hal Geordie? He was at 29.

I heard, I'll tell you where I think I heard Hal Geordie, let's see. I heard Hal Geordie when he was playing in a place on Canal Street. I thought he had Von Gammann who was playing drums, but I might be wrong about that. It could have been this guy that lives along the Gulf Coast, might have been playing vibes. I believe his brother plays Saxon Klan at, I don't know what the guy's name. He plays good vibes, very good.
He plays vibes and drums?
Well, I think he plays pretty good drums, but I believe he plays very, very good vibes. He's very, very good.
I don't know anybody like that over there.
His brother played Saxon Klan at, I think they'll live over there. Gee, I know them fellas just as good as I know myself.

The reason I asked about Geordie was according to the Prelude magazine, he said your sister played with Stratacos and Hal Geordie, both of them. But you might not have ever gotten a chance to hear them. You know, I'd go back and look at, you know, his father wrote for the Union magazine. And he'd tell about, every contract would be listed. If he'd worked for Captain Perrin or Tasso. I don't know who Captain Perrin was, but they'd have that name in the Union book. And of course that would be Emil Tasso, I guess.
Emil Tasso, yeah.
And the Musicians Ball, it tells about how he'd work on that reception committee. Did you go to those balls when they happened?
I'll tell you the truth, I don't remember too much about the balls.
What- . . . .

A few more questions because it's getting after 5 o'clock. I don't want to stay too late. But your sister, I read about her in Julie Huth, do you know that name? Oh, Julie Hooth. Julie Hooth. Who was she?

Well, she played with the band in Chicago too. Oh, I see. Oh wait, you see, Lucille at this time was in Europe, in Germany maybe. Julie Hooth was playing with her grand, I think around New York, and they cabled, what we could understand, they cabled Lucille to come back into New York and they were going on a job. Oh, I see. And the job was in Patterson, New Jersey, across the river, you know, and that's when they were at the rehearsal, coming from rehearsal, you see, the bus, we understand that a bus hit the call that they were in, and that's when Lucille got hurt, and that was in. She never did come out of that. That's when she died, around 1931, am I? 1931. Well, Julie Hooth played guitar, I believe, banjo or guitar or something, yeah.
Well this told about Max Fink at the little club?

Well Max Fink was at the little club after I played with him at the Farbackers, this was later on, just later on, yeah. When I played with Max Fink was around 1920, something like that, around that time. You're talking about a later date.

Well, it told about, you know, how they had an act. But, you know, the prelude just didn't tell much, they had a, what, a Howl column, you know, the picture of the Howl. I don't know if you remember that, and anyway, it told about all that. Let's see, what else we've got. Did you work much with Raymond Burke?
The only thing I played with Raymond was a few spot jobs, that's about all, yeah.
Just sharing there. And what about, who is Sidney Wilson?

Sidney Wilson was one of the finest piano players I've ever played. He played in the Palace Theatre. For years he was great. Very good friend of mine too, for many years. He used to come out and see us, and of course he's living, I believe, last we heard he was supposed to be living in Baton Rouge. We used to, well he called us quite a bit and then later on he, you know, we'd have to call him, he couldn't use the phone or something like that, he had to have somebody else come and get the dialed numbers. But we kept in touch with him for many, many years. Until he left town. Until he left town, yes. Great piano, one of the greatest. Great for that Baltimore stuff. Played the Palace Theatre, sure did.
And you showed me pictures of Morris Music Shops, of Morris Music School. What was that, this music school?

Well, I went to work for Morris Music School, a shop, house they call it, and manager in charge of the band instrument department, I handled that. And then later on, I organized a school, and that was a big thing around New Orleans for many years. In fact, I had a fella came down from Cleveland, and invited me to come up and spend some time on his yacht. Yeah. Well, it was something that, you see, I had, I had worked on this thing quite a while, about this free instruments, you know what I mean? Free instrument deal, you know, dollar a week and free instruments, you know, and lessons and all, see. And I knew how much, you know, instruments cost, I knew how much you could buy them for and everything else. And I presented the, you know, a thing to him and he said, well make me a proposition. And I did. Yeah. Well, talking about Morris Music's house, he is the one that, when Louis Armstrong was a little boy, Morris had a coal wagon. And Louis Armstrong used to have the bucket run around and, you know, sell the coal, you know, deliver the coal around, you know, while they were. That's in Louis Armstrong's book, incidentally, but Morris used to tell me about that quite a bit too.
And, uh, that's a Karnofsky family.
Karnofsky, K-A-R-N-O-S-K-Y. Called Karno's now. Yeah. Yeah, Karnofsky, yeah.
Nick is still busy.

Oh, he's a wonderful guy. Oh, yeah, when I went in business on Clayman Street, he used to come down and see me. Oh, and every time he wanted me to come over and see, you know, to stop over, he said, stop over and see me. Well, at that time, they went after, see, they had a fire on Ramport Street. And they got a lot of damage to start getting, and they moved in a location around, I think it was Perdita and Drive, the Dread and Drive, upstairs. We handled the business there for a while, and then I decided I wanted to go back. I didn't like it that, I didn't like it that way. And he always told me, he said, if I ever needed anything, come on and see him, you know. But sometimes he wanted me to come up and see him, and he'd say to me, he said, when he'd get a customer in the store, he'd say to me, let me see you go make that sale. And I was pretty lucky for him, I could really make sales, you know. I knew the business very well. But we got along pretty good, he was great. In fact, I saw him not too long before he had died, and he looked great. I told him, I said, oh. He had called me up and told me that it was around the war time, in the 40s, and he told me that he had sold a lot of saxophones to the government, you know. And he said, a few of them came back, and he said he didn't know why they came back. So he asked me if I'd take a look at them for him. Sure, sure, so he sent a truck out, and they were just minor things, you know, nothing to it. And he always said to me, I want to pay you, you see, and I'd say, well you don't owe me anything, you know. He said, you don't owe me anything, there wasn't anything to it. And so he kept on asking me, I want to see you, I want to see you. And so I went around the store, and he said to me, he said, I want to pay you. I said, well you don't owe me anything. He said, well, I want to give you something. I said, whatever will make you feel any better. I said, give me five dollars. He said, five dollars? He said, no, no. He said, tell me how much you really want. I said, no, I don't want him on five dollars. I said, that's all I'll take. He said, I don't even want that to tell you the truth. And he said to the girls, he said, here's a man, he said, don't want to take any money. I said, that's true, I don't take any money for nothing. And I said to him, I said, man, I said, Morris, you sure look great. I said, gee, this is the finest I've ever seen you look. He told me, he said, I'm in bad shape. He said, I got a, I think he said he had a bad heart, he told me or something. And I thought he was kidding. Wasn't too long after that, that he had passed away. He was a fine guy, I tell you, boy. Of all the guys I've ever seen, he was one of the finest. Ain't no question about that. Great guy to work for. And a man, you know, really a man.
And who was your, did any of those pupils ever become famous? From the Morris Music School?

Well I think one of them fellas started out there was a fella by name of Patterson, became a fine saxophone, but I guess there were others, I didn't keep up too much with him. But I remember he used to come around and see me around the store all the time. He played great. All the guys used to go, he was playing in some dance hall around Royal Street somewhere, and all the white guys used to go around and listen to him play, played great. John Patterson I think his name was. His dad had a hotel up on Ramport Street eight years ago. I think John was, he started on clarinet I think, but the other guys too, but I tell you, I'd...
You forget them.

Well I mean you'd see them around, they'd say, man you remember me? You know, and I started at the Morris Music School. But if we were doing good, if it wouldn't have been for the fire I probably would have stood on, and that thing would have been, got to be one of the biggest things of all. Because a guy from Cleveland, they came down to see me, he said, boy, this is one of the greatest things I've ever seen. He said, when you get your vacation, he said, come on up to Cleveland, I'll take you on my yacht, you know. He said, listen to this stuff, take me on a yacht, man.
Oh yeah?
And, yeah, but he was a great guy in the work for, I liked him very much, very much. Very true.
They listed your father's people in this article in that Basin Street magazine.

My father taught just about everybody was good. You see, my dad wanted me to be a percussionist. Well, there wasn't any room for a percussionist. I wanted to play, after you play with fellas like Ricky Tom, Stale, and Dave Perkins, and guys like that, they want you to play. They don't want you to percussion nothing, they want you to play. Like one night I'm playing at a spot there, there's a fella by the name of Brian Gilbert. I don't know if you've ever heard of him, the guy was terrific.
I knew him.
Oh, you did?
He came back and he was playing guitar when he came back.

Oh Lord, I wish I'd have seen him. Well anyway, him and Teddy, see, Gilbert was blind, but I believe Gilbert could see from the corner of his island. Now, I'm not certain about that, but I think, I remember he used to look up and say, well, Teddy had one leg, Teddy Miller.
Yeah, I made my first dollar playing music with him.

And then later he had no legs, Teddy. He had one leg, you see they used to play in front of, on Dauphin and Canal there, by Maison Blanche, for pickups. And of course, I used to, well, when I was playing over the Palisadean Lyric, I used to pass, I used to, oh, any time I was around there, I used to always go around and listen to them, they sound good. And he could make up songs and all, Gilbert, you know. So one day he said to me, he said, I want you to meet my mother. I said, gee, that's fine. So they were living over around that section, around the Pontalba apartment, around that section over there. I don't know if it was, that's long, twenty, nineteen, eighteen, twenty, way back. His mother, man, I couldn't see his mother, I said, Black had a pretty thing, they had a baby grand piano. And he said, Mom, I want you to play for him. She played, you know, good, you know, real good stuff. And he told her who I was and everything. And one night I'm playing a job with a band, Bill Krieger's playing, Bill Krieger. And man, we're playing, and man, I don't know who else we had in the band. I believe my uncle was playing six string guitar, banjo. And man, he's up there all night, see, and he's howling. He's blowing, you see, he's blowing in his horn, hand like a cornet, you know, rocking like this. He's standing up rocking back and forth, and he's howling, Peterson, you're making them melodies pop out of them drums. He said, man, let's go there all night long, see. And he don't get down, blind yell at it, see. All night long he's blowing in these, you know, like a trumpet. Man, he could get them sounds, you'd be surprised the sounds he could get out of there. With his hands cupped like that, see. And I said, boy, listen to this, that's all he was on all night. But he was great, I liked him very much. But somebody had told me he was in town. In fact, somebody told me they saw him around Raymond's place up there on Ross Street, huh? Yeah. And he said, Boydman Street rather. They said they seen him up there, but I never did see him. I wouldn't have right to see him. But he could, you know, he could sing and man, they sounded pretty good to them too. Teddy with the one leg with the crush and Gilbert Corsley. And they did pretty good. They picked up a few nickels there every day, you know.
And, let's see, your father's people, they listed Ray Badu.
Ray Badu, Teddy.
Adrian Gosley. Adrian Gosley. And Young Huxon.

Yeah, Huxon, that's right. He went on to California, never to come back. Never to see him anymore. What was his first name? Well, D.W. Oh, gotta tell you about D.W. He used to be on the road with Vans, see. In fact, he played with Dick Mackie, I believe, along the Gulf Coast once. D.W. Every time he'd go out on the road, see, when he'd get back in town, he'd call me up and say, I'm back in town, huh? He'd say, can you sell my drums for me? You know? Say, oh man, I said, you wouldn't want to sell your drums. I said, man, he said, oh man, I'm gonna quit. I said, you'll never quit playing music because it's too fascinating. He used to tell me, yeah, he said, it's fascinating. A dozen donuts, he said, between the band, he said, there's snow, he said, you're knee deep in snow, and he said, you're overcoaching porn, he'd tell me, you know. He said, yeah, it's fascinating. Then, first thing you know, he'd call me up and say, well, Hal, I'm going out with a band, I'll see you. And I saw him just before he went out to California. I think he was married at that time. And never heard, no, never heard from him anymore. Funny how they drifted away. Never did hear from D.W. Never heard from him anymore. And that's the way it was with fellas, you know, they'd go away, and sometimes, of course you wouldn't, or sometimes, maybe they'd write you, and you were too busy to write, or you'd write them, and then, you know, something else that, maybe the letters would get lost or something like that. Dick, we had a, we had boxes full of letters, had, used to get caught from Fosby when he was on the road with Crosby, you know. Man, every week they saw, we got caught from Fosby, every other guy. We had letters back there. We had a sort of, it smelled so bad after the storm back there. We had to get rid of all that stuff.
1965, we were all flooded.

You see, we didn't take, we didn't take all this wood to make this, put it up this, you know, in the back there, racks and all that you could put it up. When we first moved out here, we moved everything, but we, I still stayed in the storm until October the 1st. We moved out here in June. In September we had that storm. And that side of our garage there, one side is the, you got the, well, the slay asbestos, the slates, and the other side is the tapollion, you know. And boy, it just, and not only that, but the water came in back there about a foot, about a foot high. And it not only came from this way, but it came in that way too. And man, it's... From the top and the sides. Yeah. And George, we lost the books we had, we lost a lot of records. We lost a lot of records. We had records, we had a lot of records, the phonograph records, and things. We lost a lot of things.

Yeah, I'd like to have gotten out there and seen your stuff, you know. Gosh. That was such an awful storm. It rained and, come through four floors. Yeah, man, it sure was Karen. And I was wearing my white shampoos.
What a funny thing, man. If I'd left your stuff up on... Yeah. Yeah.
